claims.text: At high temperatures, high-entropy nanoalloy stability is primarily governed by an interplay between configurational entropy stabilization and atomic-size-driven diffusion kinetics.
Configurational entropy is relevant to phase formation in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic size difference is relevant to phase formation in high-entropy alloys.
Larger atomic size mismatch accelerates grain-boundary diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Accelerated grain-boundary diffusion produces localized elemental segregation.
Localized elemental segregation causes early phase instability.
Two nanoalloys can have identical overall elemental composition while differing primarily in atomic size mismatch.
Identical overall composition gives the two samples similar configurational entropy.
Annealing above 1000°C but below the melting temperature will sufficiently activate the relevant diffusion processes.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion causes differential atomic migration.
Differential atomic migration leads to localized segregation that can trigger phase demixing and grain coarsening.
Nanoalloys with minimal atomic size mismatch retain a more uniform composition and a more stable phase structure under otherwise identical annealing conditions.
Relative to the minimal-mismatch baseline, the larger-mismatch nanoalloy will exhibit greater grain-boundary segregation.
Relative to the minimal-mismatch baseline, the larger-mismatch nanoalloy will exhibit more pronounced phase demixing.
Relative to the minimal-mismatch baseline, the larger-mismatch nanoalloy will exhibit accelerated grain coarsening.
The effect of atomic size mismatch on diffusion kinetics and phase stability depends on exact alloy composition and nanostructure.

contradictions.description: The comparison requires identical overall elemental composition while also requiring different atomic size mismatch. Atomic size-mismatch parameters are ordinarily determined by elemental identities and fractions, so changing mismatch substantially while holding composition identical is not operationally explained and may be impossible under the proposed design.
